These hidden markups can significantly inflate your monthly operating expenses, eroding the thin margins essential to restaurant profitability.

deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Uncontrolled Operating Expenses

For restaurant operators, the Common Area Maintenance (CAM) clause is often the most volatile component of a commercial lease. While base rent is predictable, CAM charges are subject to the landlord's discretion and the shifting costs of property management. The primary danger lies in the definition of Operating Expenses, which landlords frequently draft to include nearly any cost associated with the property's upkeep.

A common predatory tactic involves the inclusion of capital improvements within the annual CAM reconciliation. Under a poorly drafted lease, a landlord may attempt to pass through the full cost of a structural repair—such as a new HVAC system or a complete parking lot resurfacing—as an operating expense. While these improvements technically benefit the property's value, they are fundamentally capital expenditures, not routine maintenance. Without explicit language excluding capital improvements, you may find yourself paying for the landlord's long-term asset appreciation through your monthly operating budget.

  • Administrative Fee Padding: Landlords often add a percentage-based management fee on top of actual costs, which can be applied to even the most basic services.
  • Permissible vs. Impermissible Costs: Ensure the lease distinguishes between routine repairs and structural replacements.
  • The Gross-up Trap: If the building is not yet fully occupied, landlords may gross up expenses to reflect a full building, which can artificially inflate your share of the costs.

Securing Market-Standard Protections

To protect your restaurant's margins, your lease must contain specific, enforceable limitations. First, demand a Cap on Controllable Expenses. This limits the year-over-year increase of expenses within your control, such as landscaping or cleaning, to a fixed percentage, such as five percent. Second, ensure that all capital expenditures are explicitly excluded from the definition of Operating Expenses unless they are specifically required by law or are necessary to maintain the property in its current condition.

Finally, never sign a lease without a robust Audit Right clause. This allows you, or your representative, to inspect the landlord's books and records to verify that the CAM charges being passed through are accurate and comply with the lease terms. Protecting your bottom line requires proactive scrutiny of these clauses before the ink is dry.
